claim: A rate-of-rise alarm warns of river surges earlier than a fixed level alarm.
data_label: open data: FOEN/BAFU 10-min and daily; simulated surges
stats: earlier than a fixed alarm, real surge
limit: Not verified on a real glacial-lake outburst; not an official warning system.
alt: Dark chart. Top: a real river surge in the Weisse Lutschine on 25 October 2026, with a green rate-of-rise alarm line 1.5 hours before the red fixed-level alarm line. Bottom: simulated 5x surges, hours of earlier warning versus rise time.
post:
A glacial lake can empty in hours, and a level sensor downstream only raises its voice once the river is already high. I built a small open-source rate-of-rise alarm for exactly that case: it watches how fast the level climbs, not how high it is.

It combines a rate-of-rise rule, a CUSUM change detector, a simple travel-time estimate to points downstream, and a sampling rule that speeds up only while the water rises, to save battery on low-power sensors.

Measured numbers: on a real 10-minute surge in the Weisse Lutschine (25 October 2026, open FOEN/BAFU data) it fired 1.5 hours before a fixed level alarm. On 40 years of daily data from 14 glacier-fed gauges, dry-weather false alarms were 0.09 per station-year in the 2001-2020 test years. In simulation, adaptive sampling needed 62 percent fewer samples.

What is not verified: I found no open high-resolution record of a real glacial-lake outburst, so those surges are simulated. Rain floods also trigger the alarm, and at stations with daily hydropower releases it fires far too often. It is not an official warning system.

Would you trust a rate-based alarm over a level alarm at your site, and what would you want to see first?

Code: https://github.com/Usernamepersonperson/lake-outburst-alarm
